title: Bounded choices in every lesson
statement: Build a few bounded, meaningful choices into every lesson, such as which text or question comes first and how to respond, so learners bring their interests into it.
example: The video's guidance is five choices in every lesson, not once a day.
detail: An IES video on improving reading comprehension from kindergarten to grade 3, quoted in a reading course's review standard, recommends five choices every lesson rather than once a day, because choice brings the student's interests, competencies and self into the lesson (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/g3-reading-red-team/references/teaching-moves/motivation-levers.md`). The standard's design gives each lesson a fixed set of bounded choices, which text from a curated set, which part to read first and how to respond, so their presence can be audited, and never offers a free choice of anything to read. It is practice guidance in a video, not a trial result.
against: The effect was weaker for adults than for children, and the stage-environment-fit source was read only as an abstract summary because its full text was blocked (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, lines 110 and 30).

evidence.quote: Good teachers are giving five choices every lesson; not just once a day, but every lesson five choices brings the student's interests, the student's competencies, the student's self into the lesson.
every lesson exposes a fixed set of bounded choices — which text (from a curated set), which part to read first, response mode (say / draw / type)
A meta-analysis of 41 studies found choice raised intrinsic motivation, effort, task performance and perceived competence.
The effect was strongest with 2–4 successive choices and weaker for adults than for children.
Offer a small number of meaningful choices: which text or question first, typed or spoken answer, hint now or later, audio on or off.
Give students real decisions: which question to tackle, when to move on, whether to hear audio.

citations.ref: Improving Reading Comprehension in Kindergarten Through 3rd Grade, Part 5, IES video
